extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, instructors, and others studying student reasoning about proofs (undergraduate combinatorics/proof pedagogy)
extracted.subtask_description: Qualitative analysis of how undergraduate students characterize and evaluate combinatorial (enumerative) proofs using Harel & Sowder's proof-scheme framework; identifies which proof schemes students use and which features make combinatorial arguments feel (un)rigorous to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof (enumerative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof that directly involves counting (enumerative argument): shows equality by exhibiting that both sides count the same set of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout as the target proof type. Authors note that while the binomial theorem can be considered combinatorial in context, here 'combinatorial proof' specifically means an enumerative counting argument. Examples: splitting 2n objects into two groups or counting committees with/without a particular individual. Combinatorial proofs can be rigorous but students may view them as intuitive or informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformational proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student accepts an argument as proof when it transforms the conjecture into facts—e.g., showing each side counts the same outcomes; refinement/precision of definitions makes the argument feel like a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by comprehension and use of a proof heuristic that renders conjectures into facts. Example: Riley would accept the combinatorial argument as proof after refining variable definitions so no conceivable counterexample remains. Emerged clearly in interviews as students who accept enumerative arguments when specified precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student judges proofs by ritualistic, surface-level features (length, formal symbols, familiar algebraic/inductive structure) rather than by soundness of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students attended to appearance (presence of symbols, formal structure, length). Example: Peyton thought a combinatorial argument 'was just words' and 'not formal enough' because it lacked algebra/induction and mathematical symbols. The scheme explains resistance to accept enumerative proofs that are short or non-symbolic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual restrictive proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student interprets and proves conjectures in terms of a specific context; treats a proof as valid only within that context rather than as a general argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harel & Sowder example: proving a statement about n-dimensional vector spaces by reasoning only in R^n. In this study, students sometimes accepted a combinatorial argument only when it used a particular context (e.g., numbered set {1,...,n+1} or committee examples) and felt it was less general or 'arbitrary'. This led to coding of contextual restrictive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritarian external conviction proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student's main source of conviction is authority (textbook, teacher, TA); acceptance depends on whether an authority would endorse the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Riley believed a combinatorial proof could be valid but said they would not turn it in because TAs might mark it down for being too short. This scheme explains when students judge proofs relative to imagined evaluators rather than on mathematical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student relies on perceptual observations and rudimentary mental images (intuition) that give a sense something is true but lack transformational justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students described combinatorial arguments as providing intuition ('this is my intuition') but not as formal proofs. Authors associate statements that combinatorial proofs 'explain' but do not 'prove' with the perceptual scheme. Example: Adrien and Peyton distinguishing intuition from formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student convinces themselves by manipulating symbols without reference to their functional or quantitative meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by Harel & Sowder as symbolic manipulation detached from meaning. The paper notes this scheme is unlikely in combinatorial-proof contexts (because combinatorial proofs typically do not involve such symbolic manipulation) and found no evidence of its emergence in the interviews, though algebraic verification sometimes occurred outside the enumerative representation system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student establishes truth by quantitatively evaluating special cases (e.g., base case and n->n+1), using such evaluations as conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harel & Sowder described this as using special cases to persuade. The authors note inductive reasoning is unlikely to be used within enumerative (combinatorial) representation but may coexist when students switch to algebraic methods; no clear emergence in the data for combinatorial-proof reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectures are interpreted in general terms but the student's proof is expressed in a particular (often concrete) context or with specific numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: substituting specific values for variables to reason about a general identity. Authors note this could be used as a heuristic but they did not observe it in this study because participants were asked to prove in terms of the original variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof scheme appropriate for existence theorems where the student constructs an example or object to demonstrate existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By definition applies to existence proofs; combinatorial binomial identities are not existence statements, so this scheme was unlikely and not observed in the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Student uses axioms or appeals directly to axiomatic foundations as the source of conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harel & Sowder include this scheme but authors found no evidence of its emergence in interviews (possibly due to sample size). It remains a plausible scheme in other contexts where students reference axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbols/algebra/induction as markers of 'mathematical proof'
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often view presence of algebraic manipulations, formal symbols, or induction as necessary markers that an argument counts as 'real' mathematics or a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple students (e.g., Peyton) explicitly said combinatorial arguments 'have no math to back me up' and that 'there's no algebra or induction'—indicating they expect symbolic/algebraic structure for proofs. This expectation can cause them to reject otherwise valid enumerative proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length, explicitness, and avoidance of leaving details to reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Students judge rigor partly by how detailed a proof is, whether variables/terms are precisely defined, and whether steps are left 'as exercises' for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adrien disliked proofs that left parts to the reader; Riley mentioned a 'critical length' expected by graders. The page discusses how leaving details implicit or failing to define terms precisely can make an argument feel non-rigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour via inability to conceive a counterexample and definitional precision
rubrics_metrics.description: A student's acceptance of an argument as proof can rest on the sense that no counterexample can be conceived if definitions are precise and the argument eliminates possible counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riley expressed that a proof, to them, means one cannot come up with a counterexample or 'conceive of the nature of a counterexample'—emphasizing the role of precision in definitions to secure conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof that explains vs proof that proves (explanatory vs justificatory criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between proofs that provide intuitive explanation ('this is why it is true') and proofs that provide formal justification guaranteeing truth in all cases ('this shows it is true for all n').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peyton and others described combinatorial proofs as offering explanation/intuition while preferring induction/algebra to 'show' truth universally. Authors connect this to literature on 'proofs that explain' and note combinatorial proofs may be judged as explanatory rather than as fully rigorous by some students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding arbitrary contextual assumptions (implicit 'without loss of generality' worries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may judge an argument as less valid if it seems to rely on an arbitrary choice (e.g., ordering or labeling) that seems unjustified or 'artificial' rather than general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adrien found using an ordering of objects 'arbitrary' and thus felt combinatorial arguments based on such an ordering were less convincing than induction. Authors note concerns about extra assumptions made 'without loss of generality' can undermine student acceptance.
